name: Adam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Adam, thanks for talking to me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and what you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, out to the ewes by half past. We've got about four hundred sheep at Hollow Oak, plus forty beef cattle and a hundred acres of oats. I check water troughs, move the electric fencing, and I'm usually the one who sorts the farm shop in the afternoon, because I'm the only one who doesn't mind the till system.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eighteen months. I was a postman for thirty years, same round on the east side of town. Sunita and I always said we'd move out to the country, and when her mum left us a bit of money we did it. Then I thought, well, I can't just sit and watch the hills, so I asked Gwen, who owns Hollow Oak, if she needed a pair of hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the problem-solving. When a ewe's off her food, I take a photo, ask the AI what it might be, then go and find Gwen and we work it out. What's hard is that I'm fifty-eight and still learning to back a trailer through a gateway. The young lad, Rhys, does it in one go while I'm on my fifth try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a good tool, not a god. I'd probably post something on the local farming group about which apps actually helped this year, because I'm always the one sharing that stuff. And I'd tell the lads that we can stop arguing about it at lunch now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, a bit of a shame. I like the stuff. I use it every day, for the shop stock, for the lambing questions, even for writing Gwen's grant forms. If it stops there, it's still useful, but I'd been hoping for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep getting better at the actual farming, because that's where I'm weakest. I'd also see if Gwen would let me set up the shop's online orders properly, using the tools we've got. Small things that save an hour here and there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a touch let down. Like a new tractor that's just the old one with a nicer seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd been hoping for more. More of what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More of the hard thinking taken off us, so I could learn faster. I've got maybe ten years of working left, and I started late. If the machines could teach me what Gwen learned in forty years, I'd catch up quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And for your neighbours and colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For them it's probably good news. Rhys wants to farm his whole life, and in this picture he can. I'd be glad for him, even if I'm a little disappointed for myself.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool, not a god, and I'd share which apps actually helped this year on the local farming group.
S0.think: Privately it's a small disappointment, because he uses AI every day and hoped it would help him catch up on forty years of know-how he never had.
S0.do: Keeps working at Hollow Oak and focuses on improving his hands-on farming. Offers to set up the farm shop's online orders with the tools already there.
S0.feel: Calm and a little let down, like a new tractor that's the old one with a nicer seat.
S0.quote: Like a new tractor that's just the old one with a nicer seat.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is the rare farm worker who's disappointed by a plateau, because he sees AI as a way to make up for starting late. He's honest that his real weakness is the hands-on side. He thinks about younger colleagues without prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to get ahead of it, not get flattened by it. I'd post about it, and I'd say at the market that farms should be getting in early and training their own people to run the new kit. And I'd say the government should help small farms afford it, not just the big estates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I've got a real opening. I'm the worst shepherd on Hollow Oak and the best one with a phone. In a strange way, that might be what saves me. If a robot comes for the fencing and the feeding, someone has to set it up and fix it when it falls over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd ask Gwen to let me trial a virtual fencing system, the collars that keep the cattle in without posts, because some farms are already using it. I'd do a short course on farm drones over the winter, maybe a few hundred out of savings if Gwen won't pay. And I'd push to get the shop's stock and orders running mostly on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly, and a bit excited. Sunita says I'm like a boy with a new bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people your age would find that a lot to take on. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I spent thirty years on a round where the machines changed everything. The sorting went automatic, the scanners came, the van got a computer that told me the route. The postmen who fought it were miserable, and the ones who learned it had an easier time. I'm not making that mistake twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at Hollow Oak lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Tony, who's been doing the fencing for Gwen part time for years. He's sixty-four and he doesn't want any of it. I'd want Gwen to keep him on for the stock work, and I'd say so to her face.

S1.say: I'd say this is the chance to get ahead of the change, that farms should train their own people on the new kit, and the government should help small farms afford it.
S1.think: He sees a real opening: weakest at shepherding, strongest with technology, he could be the one who sets up and fixes the machines when they come.
S1.do: Asks Gwen within months to trial virtual fencing collars for the cattle and takes a winter drone course, paying a few hundred from savings if needed. Pushes to automate the shop's stock and orders.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like a boy with a new bike.
S1.quote: The postmen who fought it were miserable, and the ones who learned it had an easier time.
S1.fieldNote: Adam's confidence comes from lived experience at the post office, not from theory. He'd still speak up for Tony, an older colleague who doesn't want change, which fits his progressive views. His self-assessment, worst shepherd and best with a phone, sums up his strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a robot dividend, a share of what these machines save paid back to people, and we need it before it arrives, not after. I'd say it online, in the farming groups, and I'd go to meetings. I'd be loud about it, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it shakes me more than I'd admit. I'd be sixty when it lands, and even if I'm quick with the tools, there'll be a hundred young people who are quicker. If the robot can do the fencing and the feeding and the fixing, then the job of being the guy who fixes the robot is gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years learning everything I could, every system Gwen could afford to try, so I'm the one she can't do without. I'd also sell some of the things I make, like the online shop setups, to other small farms on the side. And we'd stop the plan to replace the car and keep that money as a cushion, so we'd have maybe six months instead of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got some skills that would matter for a while, but anxious. It's the first picture where I can't see the shape of my own place in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it shakes you more than you'd admit. Who wouldn't you admit it to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunita, probably. She worries enough for both of us, and she's at the pharmacy counter, which would change too. I'd tell her I'm on top of it, and then I'd sit up at night reading about what other countries are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning get you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. It's enough to learn one or two systems, not to become anyone new. For a lad of twenty-five, two years is a whole apprenticeship. For me it's a couple of lambing seasons.

S2.say: I'd say we need a robot dividend, a share of what machines save paid back to people, set up before AGI arrives. I'd say it loudly online and at meetings.
S2.think: It shakes him more than he'd admit: at 60, younger people will be quicker, and if robots fix robots, his planned role disappears too.
S2.do: Spends the two years learning every system Gwen can trial so he's indispensable, and sells online shop setups to other small farms on the side. Drops the plan to replace the car to stretch savings from about four to six months.
S2.feel: Anxious rather than panicked, because for the first time he can't see his own place.
S2.quote: For a lad of twenty-five, two years is a whole apprenticeship. For me it's a couple of lambing seasons.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-comfortable person in his household gets anxious when the timeline is this short, because his age cancels out his skills. He hides it from Sunita, a clear gap between say and think. His politics get sharper here, with a specific ask for a robot dividend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, and I'd be pushing farms and the college to set up proper training in running these machines. I'd volunteer to help teach the older ones if they wanted, because I'm one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, which feels much better. That's long enough to properly learn the machine side and be useful till I stop. I'd probably work till sixty-six or so as the person who looks after the systems on two or three farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do a proper course in farm robotics at the college, the evening one. I'd put a few thousand into a drone of my own and start doing crop surveys for neighbours, because they'll want them before they've got their own. Once AGI arrives I'd go part time at Hollow Oak and do the rest as a contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe, but mostly I'd feel I had a chance. It's like the gap between a gate closing on you and a gate you can see closing from across the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A few thousand is a big share of your savings. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a real plan with a real risk. Sunita would want it to pay for itself in the first year or I stop. I'd agree to that. If the drone doesn't earn its keep, it gets sold and the money goes back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently than in the fast picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one I'm just trying to stay on my feet. With five years I can build something. That's the difference: grabbing on, or getting a foothold.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, and I'd push farms and the college for proper machine training, and volunteer to help teach older workers.
S3.think: Five years puts him at 63, long enough to learn the machine side properly and stay useful until about 66 looking after systems on a few farms.
S3.do: Takes an evening course in farm robotics in year one and puts a few thousand into a drone to do crop surveys for neighbours, selling it if it doesn't pay off in a year. Goes part time at Hollow Oak and contracts once AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, like seeing a gate closing from across the field rather than having it close on him.
S3.quote: That's the difference: grabbing on, or getting a foothold.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turns Adam from defensive to entrepreneurial. He's willing to risk real savings but sets a clear stop rule with Sunita, which shows his risk-taking isn't reckless. He sees himself as a teacher for other older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, we've got a decade, so let's make it fair. Shared machines, training for everyone, and the savings spread around. I'd say it everywhere, online, at the market, to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd be sixty-eight and planning to stop anyway. If anything, I'd get to see the exciting bit from the inside, setting up the first robots at Hollow Oak, then hand over to someone younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning, one new system each year, and help Gwen choose which ones to buy so she doesn't waste money on the flashy ones. I'd join the local farming group's tech committee. And I'd put a bit by for retirement, because there's no rush now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, even. It's the picture where I get to be part of it without it costing me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Priya is thirty and works in insurance, and she's the one who'd worry me. I'd tell her to start now, find the part of her work that needs a person in the room, and get good at that. Ten years is plenty if you start in year one, and almost nothing if you start in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything in that picture still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who owns the robots. If it's Gwen and farms like hers, fine. If it's one big company renting them out and taking a slice of every lamb, that's the bit I'd fight.

S4.say: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's make it fair: shared machines, training for everyone, and the savings spread around.
S4.think: He's fine: he'd be 68 and stopping anyway, and he'd get to help set up the first robots at Hollow Oak before handing over.
S4.do: Learns one new system a year, helps Gwen pick sensible machines, and joins the local farming group's tech committee. Puts money aside for retirement.
S4.feel: Calm and curious, part of the change without it costing him much.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty if you start in year one, and almost nothing if you start in year nine.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Adam relaxes and turns to fairness and his daughter Priya's job. His one sharp worry is ownership, specifically a single company renting out robots and taking a cut. He's consistent: the same instinct to learn early runs through every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Even someone like me who loves the stuff needs time, and two years at sixty is nothing. What would help is paid, local training for older farm workers to run and fix the new machines, and a share of what the robots save coming back to the people they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be a beginner at fifty-eight. Everybody assumes older people hate new things. I love new things. What I hate is being slow at the old things, the trailer and the gates. The machines might actually even that out for people like me.

headlineQuote: I'm the worst shepherd on Hollow Oak and the best one with a phone. In a strange way, that might be what saves me.
portrait: Adam Baker is 58, a former postman who moved to the country with his partner Sunita and has spent 18 months as a junior hand at Hollow Oak, a sheep, beef and oats farm with a farm shop. His hands-on skills are still behind, but he uses AI tools every day, for lambing questions, weed photos and the shop's stock, and he enjoys new kit. He leans left and wants the gains from robots shared through public policy, but his first move in every scenario is to become the person who runs the machines. He stays calm through a plateau and steady change, gets anxious with AGI in two years because he'd be a 60-year-old competing for the few machine-minder jobs, and relaxes again as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even an early adopter needs time, and two years would leave him a 60-year-old beginner competing with younger people for the few jobs looking after the machines.
whatWouldHelp: Paid, local training for older farm workers to run and repair the new machines, and a share of the savings from robots going back to the people they replace.
